title: TypeScript
summary: Add a powerful type system to JavaScript: annotations, interfaces, unions, narrowing, generics, classes and utility types, with a judged exercise in every lesson.

lessons.title: Why TypeScript? Your first typed program
lessons.summary: See what TypeScript adds to JavaScript and write your first type annotations.

slides.title: JavaScript with types
slides.text:
**TypeScript** = JavaScript + **types**.
- Every JS program is (almost) valid TS
- Types catch mistakes **before** you run the code
- Types are removed when the code runs
slides.narration:
TypeScript is JavaScript with one superpower: types.
You describe what kind of values your variables and functions expect, and the TypeScript checker warns you about mistakes before the code ever runs.
When the program runs, the types are simply stripped away, leaving plain JavaScript.

slides.title: Type annotations
slides.text: Add `: type` after a name.
slides.narration:
A type annotation is a colon followed by a type, written after a variable name.
Here city must always be a string. If you try to store a number in it, your editor underlines it in red right away.

slides.title: Type inference
slides.text: Often you do **not** need to write the type. TS **infers** it.
slides.code:
let count = 10;       // inferred: number
const greeting = 'hi'; // inferred: 'hi'
count = 'ten';        // Error!
slides.narration:
TypeScript is smart. When you assign a value right away, it figures out the type for you. This is called inference.
A good rule is to let TypeScript infer simple variables, and to write types for function parameters and for data shapes.

slides.title: How your code runs here
slides.text:
In Averroes Code your `.ts` file is run by Node.js, which **strips the types** and runs the JavaScript.
Read input with:
slides.narration:
In this course, your TypeScript runs on Node.js, which removes the types and runs the result.
To read standard input, import readFileSync from the node colon fs module and read file number zero.
For type checking, your editor is your friend: hover over names to see their types.

slides.title: Erasable syntax only
slides.text:
We stick to type syntax that can simply be **erased**:
- no `enum`, no `namespace`
- no constructor parameter properties
Modern TS projects increasingly follow this rule too.
slides.narration:
One more note. A few older TypeScript features, like enums and namespaces, generate extra JavaScript code instead of just disappearing.
Node's type stripping does not support them, so this course uses only erasable syntax. You will learn modern replacements, such as union types, that work even better.

lessons.notes:
## What is TypeScript?

TypeScript (TS) is a **superset of JavaScript** made by Microsoft. It adds a static type system: you describe the shape of your data and the TypeScript compiler (`tsc`) or your editor checks that the code uses it correctly.

- Types are checked **before** running (at "compile time").
- Types are **erased** at runtime: the program that runs is plain JavaScript.
- Big projects (VS Code, Angular, many React apps) use TS because it catches bugs early and makes code easier to navigate.

## Basic annotations

```typescript
let name: string = 'Ada';
let age: number = 36;
let active: boolean = true;
let nothing: null = null;
let notSet: undefined = undefined;
```

## Inference

```typescript
let score = 0;        // number
const lang = 'TS';    // the literal type 'TS'
```

Let TypeScript infer obvious types; annotate function parameters and public APIs.

## Running TypeScript

- `tsc file.ts` type-checks and converts to JavaScript.
- Modern Node.js can run `.ts` files directly by **stripping** types (`node --experimental-strip-types file.ts`, on by default in newer versions). It does **not** type-check; the editor or `tsc --noEmit` does that.

Read input like this:

```typescript
import { readFileSync } from 'node:fs';
const input: string = readFileSync(0, 'utf8');
```

## Erasable syntax only

Type stripping can only remove type syntax. Features that generate code, such as `enum`, `namespace` and constructor parameter properties (`constructor(private x: number)`), are not supported. TypeScript 5.8 added the `erasableSyntaxOnly` option to enforce this. We will use unions of string literals instead of enums.

## any and unknown

`any` turns type checking off for a value: avoid it. `unknown` means "could be anything, check before using it", which is the safe choice.

quiz.q: What happens to TypeScript types when the program runs?
quiz.explain: Types exist only for checking. The running code is plain JavaScript.

quiz.q: let x = 5; What type does TypeScript infer for x?
quiz.explain: The initial value 5 is a number, so x is inferred as number.

quiz.q: Which feature is NOT erasable and is avoided in this course?
quiz.explain: enum generates runtime code, so simple type stripping cannot handle it.

exercise.title: Typed greeting
exercise.prompt:
Input: line 1 is a name, line 2 is a year of birth.

Store the name in a `string` variable and the year in a `number` variable (use annotations), then print:
```
Hello, NAME!
In 2026 you turn AGE.
```
where AGE = 2026 - year.

tests.output:
Hello, Mei Lin!
In 2026 you turn 0.

lessons.title: Typing functions
lessons.summary: Annotate parameters and return types, use optional and default parameters, and type callbacks.

slides.title: Parameter and return types
slides.text: Parameters **need** types. The return type comes after `)`.
slides.narration:
Function parameters are the most important place to write types, because TypeScript cannot guess what callers will pass.
The return type is written after the closing parenthesis. Now passing a string by mistake is caught immediately.

slides.title: Optional and default parameters
slides.text:
- `name?: string` may be left out (it is then `undefined`)
- `x = 10` default value, type inferred
slides.narration:
A question mark after a parameter name makes it optional, and its type becomes string or undefined.
A default value makes a parameter optional too, and TypeScript infers its type from the default.

slides.title: Arrow functions and function types
slides.text: Describe a function's **shape** with `(params) => ReturnType`.
slides.narration:
Functions are values, so they have types too.
A function type looks like an arrow function: the parameters in parentheses, an arrow, then the return type.
When a variable has a function type, TypeScript infers the parameter types of the arrow function for you.

slides.title: void and never
slides.text:
- `void`: returns nothing useful
- `never`: never returns (throws or loops forever)
slides.narration:
Two special return types. void means the function does not return a useful value, like a logger.
never means the function never finishes normally, because it always throws an error.

slides.title: Rest parameters and overload-free design
slides.text: Rest parameters are typed as arrays.
slides.narration:
Rest parameters collect any number of arguments, so their type is an array, like number array.
Simple, clearly typed functions like this are easier to use than functions that try to accept everything.

quiz.q: Where is the return type of a function written?
options: After the closing ) of the parameters
quiz.explain: function f(x: number): string { ... } places the return type after the parameter list.

quiz.q: What is the type of name in function f(name?: string)?
quiz.explain: An optional parameter may be missing, so it can also be undefined.

quiz.q: Which return type fits a function that always throws?
quiz.explain: never means the function never returns normally.

exercise.title: Typed math helpers
exercise.prompt:
Write three typed functions:
- `average(nums: number[]): number`
- `clamp(value: number, min: number, max: number): number` (limits value to the range)
- `format(n: number, digits = 2): string` (returns `n.toFixed(digits)`)

Input: line 1 has numbers separated by spaces; line 2 has `min max`.

Print:
```
average: AVG
clamped: AVG_CLAMPED
```
where both values are formatted with 2 decimals.

lessons.title: Arrays, tuples and readonly
lessons.summary: Type lists with T[], fixed-size pairs with tuples, and protect data with readonly.

slides.title: Typed arrays
slides.text: `number[]` or `Array<number>`: a list of numbers.
slides.narration:
An array type is written as the item type followed by square brackets.
You can also write Array with angle brackets. Both mean the same thing.
Now TypeScript makes sure only numbers end up in the scores array.

slides.title: Tuples
slides.text: A **tuple** is an array with a **fixed length** and a type for each position.
slides.narration:
Sometimes an array has a fixed shape, like a point with an x and a y, or a pair of a name and a count.
A tuple type lists the type of each position. Destructuring a tuple gives each variable its correct type.

slides.title: readonly
slides.text: `readonly` arrays cannot be changed.
slides.narration:
Marking an array as readonly removes all the methods that change it, such as push and sort.
This is great for data that should never be modified by accident. You can still make changed copies.

slides.title: as const
slides.text: `as const` makes the narrowest, readonly type.
slides.narration:
Adding as const after a literal tells TypeScript to keep the exact values and make everything readonly.
Combined with typeof, you can turn a list of values into a union type. This is the modern replacement for enums.

quiz.q: Which type describes an array of strings?
quiz.explain: string[] (or Array<string>) is an array of any length containing strings.

quiz.q: What is [string, number]?
options: An array of strings or numbers
A tuple: first a string, then a number
quiz.explain: A tuple has a fixed length and a type for each position.

quiz.q: const c = ['red', 'blue'] as const; What is (typeof c)[number]?
quiz.explain: as const keeps literal types, and indexing with number gives the union of the elements.

exercise.title: Min and max with a tuple
exercise.prompt:
Write `minMax(values: readonly number[]): [number, number]` returning the smallest and largest value as a tuple.

Input: several lines, each with integers separated by spaces.

For each line, destructure the tuple and print `min=LO max=HI range=HI-LO`.

tests.output:
min=5 max=5 range=0
min=-8 max=4 range=12

min=7 max=7 range=0
min=0 max=100 range=100

lessons.title: Object types and interfaces
lessons.summary: Describe the shape of objects with type aliases and interfaces, including optional and readonly properties.

slides.title: Describing object shapes
slides.text: An **object type** lists properties and their types.
slides.narration:
Most real data is made of objects. An object type lists each property and its type.
The type keyword creates a type alias, a name you can reuse everywhere.
If you forget a property or misspell one, TypeScript tells you.

slides.title: Interfaces
slides.text: `interface` is another way to name an object shape.
slides.narration:
An interface does almost the same job as a type alias for objects.
Many teams use interface for object shapes and type for everything else. Either choice is fine; just be consistent.

slides.title: Optional and readonly
slides.text:
- `?` optional property
- `readonly` cannot be reassigned
slides.narration:
A question mark makes a property optional, so the object can leave it out.
readonly means the property can be set when the object is created, but not changed afterwards.

slides.title: Extending
slides.text: Build bigger types from smaller ones.
slides.narration:
Interfaces can extend other interfaces, adding new properties.
With type aliases you get the same result using the ampersand, called an intersection, which means this and also that.

slides.title: Index signatures and Record
slides.text: Objects used as **dictionaries**:
slides.narration:
Sometimes you do not know the keys in advance, for example when counting words.
Record of string to number describes an object whose keys are strings and whose values are numbers. An index signature says the same thing in longer form.

quiz.q: What does ? after a property name mean?
quiz.explain: A question mark marks an optional property.

quiz.q: TypeScript checks objects by...
quiz.explain: TypeScript uses structural typing: matching shape is what counts.

quiz.q: What does Record<string, number> describe?
options: An object with string keys and number values
quiz.explain: Record<K, V> is an object type with keys K and values V.

exercise.title: Inventory report
exercise.prompt:
Define an interface `Item` with `name: string`, `price: number` and `qty: number`.

Input: one item per line as `name price qty` (name has no spaces).

Build an `Item[]`, then print for each item `NAME: QTY x PRICE = SUBTOTAL` (subtotal with 2 decimals, price as given), and finally `TOTAL: T` with 2 decimals.

lessons.title: Union and literal types
lessons.summary: Allow several types with unions and restrict values to exact options with literal types.

slides.title: One of several types
slides.text: A **union** `A | B` means "A **or** B".
slides.code:
let id: string | number;
id = 42;      // ok
id = 'A-42';  // ok
id = true;    // Error
slides.narration:
Sometimes a value can legitimately be one of several types, like an ID that can be a number or a string.
A union type, written with a vertical bar, says exactly that.

slides.title: Literal types
slides.text: A type can be an **exact value**.
slides.narration:
A literal type is a single exact value, like the string up.
A union of literals lists every allowed option. TypeScript will reject anything else and your editor will even autocomplete the choices.

slides.title: Replacing enums
slides.text: Use literal unions instead of `enum`.
slides.narration:
Literal unions are the modern replacement for enums.
They are erased completely at runtime, they print nicely, and they work with plain strings coming from input or JSON.

slides.title: null and undefined in unions
slides.text: With `strict` mode, `null` must be **explicit**.
slides.narration:
In strict mode, null and undefined are separate types. A function that might not find something should say so with a union with null.
TypeScript then forces you to check before you use the value, which prevents the most common crash in JavaScript.

quiz.q: What does string | number mean?
options: Both a string and a number at once
Either a string or a number
A string converted to a number
quiz.explain: A union value can be any one of its members.

quiz.q: type Light = 'red' | 'green'; Which assignment is valid?
quiz.explain: Only the exact literals 'red' and 'green' are allowed (case-sensitive).

quiz.q: What does the return type x is Theme express?
options: A type predicate: if true, x is a Theme
quiz.explain: Type predicates tell TypeScript what a boolean-returning check proves.

exercise.title: Traffic commands
exercise.prompt:
Define `type Command = 'up' | 'down' | 'left' | 'right'` and a type guard `isCommand(x: string): x is Command`.

A robot starts at `(0, 0)`. Input: one word per line. For each valid command move one step (`up` adds 1 to y, `down` subtracts 1 from y, `left`/`right` change x). For an invalid word print `ignored: WORD`.

At the end print `position: (X, Y)`.

lessons.title: Narrowing: checking types safely
lessons.summary: Use typeof, instanceof, in, equality and discriminated unions to work safely with union types.

slides.title: What is narrowing?
slides.text: Inside a check, TypeScript **knows more** about a value.
slides.narration:
When you have a union, TypeScript only lets you use what all members share.
But as soon as you check the type, for example with typeof, TypeScript narrows the value inside that branch. This is called narrowing.

slides.title: typeof, instanceof, in
slides.text:
- `typeof x === 'string'` for primitives
- `x instanceof Date` for classes
- `'swim' in animal` for properties
slides.narration:
TypeScript understands several kinds of checks.
typeof works for strings, numbers and other primitives. instanceof works for class instances. And the in operator checks whether an object has a property.

slides.title: Truthiness and equality
slides.text: Checking for `null` / `undefined` narrows too.
slides.narration:
A simple if checking that a value exists removes null and undefined from the type.
Comparing with triple equals narrows as well.

slides.title: Discriminated unions
slides.text: Give each variant a **tag** property with a literal type.
slides.narration:
The most powerful pattern in TypeScript is the discriminated union.
Every variant has a shared property, often called kind or type, with a different literal value.
Switching on that property narrows the object to exactly one variant.

slides.title: Exhaustiveness with never
slides.text: Make TypeScript tell you when you forget a case.
slides.narration:
Here is a trick professionals love. In the default branch, pass the value to a function that accepts never.
If someone later adds a new shape and forgets to handle it, the value is no longer never and TypeScript reports an error.

quiz.q: Inside if (typeof x === 'number') { ... }, what is x?
quiz.explain: The typeof check narrows x to number inside the branch.

quiz.q: What makes a union "discriminated"?
options: Each member has a common property with a different literal type
quiz.explain: The shared literal property (the discriminant) lets TypeScript tell the variants apart.

quiz.q: Why pass a value to a function taking never in the default branch?
options: To get a compile error if a case is not handled
To convert it to a string
quiz.explain: If any variant is unhandled, the value is not never and compilation fails.

exercise.title: Shape areas
exercise.prompt:
Define a discriminated union `Shape` with three variants:
- `{ kind: 'circle'; radius: number }`
- `{ kind: 'rect'; width: number; height: number }`
- `{ kind: 'triangle'; base: number; height: number }`

Input: one shape per line, e.g. `circle 2`, `rect 3 4`, `triangle 6 2`.

Parse each line into a `Shape`, compute its area with a `switch` on `kind`, and print `KIND: AREA` with 2 decimals. Finally print `largest: KIND` (the first one if tied).

lessons.title: Generics
lessons.summary: Write reusable functions and types that work with any type while keeping full type safety.

slides.title: The problem
slides.text: A function that works for **any** type... without losing the type.
slides.narration:
Say you want a function that returns the first item of any array.
Using any works, but it throws away the type information, so the result is unchecked.
Generics solve this.

slides.title: Type parameters
slides.text: `<T>` is a **type variable**, filled in when the function is used.
slides.narration:
A generic function has a type parameter, usually called T, in angle brackets.
T is like a variable for types. When you call first with numbers, T becomes number, and the result is correctly typed.
You almost never have to write T yourself; TypeScript infers it.

slides.title: Generic types
slides.text: Types and interfaces can be generic too.
slides.narration:
You have already used generic types: Array of string and Record are generic.
You can write your own, like a Box that holds a value of any type, or a Pair with two type parameters.

slides.title: Constraints
slides.text: `T extends X` limits which types are allowed.
slides.narration:
Sometimes your generic code needs something from T, like a length property.
A constraint with extends says T must have at least that shape. Strings and arrays qualify, numbers do not.

slides.title: keyof with generics
slides.text: Safely read a property by name.
slides.narration: keyof T is the union of T's property names. Combined with a second type parameter, you get a function that only accepts real keys, and returns exactly the right type for each one.

quiz.q: In function f<T>(x: T): T, what is T?
quiz.explain: T is a type variable that is filled in when the function is called.

quiz.q: What does T extends { length: number } mean?
options: T must have a numeric length property
quiz.explain: The constraint requires T to have at least a length of type number.

quiz.q: For const u = { a: 1, b: 'x' }, what is keyof typeof u?
quiz.explain: keyof gives the union of the property names.

exercise.title: A generic queue
exercise.prompt:
Implement a generic class `Queue<T>` with `enqueue(item: T): void`, `dequeue(): T | undefined` and a `size` getter. Also write a generic function `last<T>(items: T[]): T | undefined`.

Input: commands, one per line:
- `add WORD` adds a word to the queue
- `next` removes the front word and prints it, or prints `empty`

At the end print `size: N` and `last added: WORD` (use `last` on an array of every added word; print `none` if none).

tests.input:
add a
add b
next
add c

tests.output:
x
empty
size: 0
last added: x

tests.input:
add one
add two
add three

lessons.title: Classes in TypeScript
lessons.summary: Type class fields, use public, private, protected and readonly, implement interfaces and write abstract classes.

slides.title: Typed fields
slides.text: Declare fields with their types at the top of the class.
slides.narration:
In TypeScript, class fields are declared with their types, usually at the top of the class.
Fields must be initialized, either directly or in the constructor. Otherwise TypeScript warns you.

slides.title: Access modifiers
slides.text:
- `public` (default): anyone
- `private`: only this class (compile-time)
- `protected`: this class and subclasses
- `#field`: truly private at runtime
slides.narration:
Access modifiers control who can use a member.
private and protected are checked by TypeScript only, and erased at runtime. The JavaScript hash syntax gives real runtime privacy.
readonly fields can be set in the constructor but never changed later.

slides.title: No parameter properties here
slides.text:
The shortcut `constructor(private x: number)` is **not erasable**.
Write the field and assign it.
slides.narration:
You may see a shortcut in older code, where a modifier in front of a constructor parameter creates a field automatically.
That feature generates extra code, so Node's type stripping cannot run it. Declare the field and assign it yourself. It is only one more line, and clearer for beginners.

slides.title: implements
slides.text: A class can promise to match an interface.
slides.narration:
implements makes a class promise to follow an interface.
If the class is missing a method, or a method has the wrong type, TypeScript reports it right on the class.

slides.title: Abstract classes
slides.text: An **abstract** class cannot be created directly; subclasses fill in the gaps.
slides.narration:
An abstract class is a partial blueprint. It can contain real methods, and abstract methods with no body.
You cannot create it with new. Instead, subclasses must implement every abstract method.

quiz.q: Which modifier is enforced at runtime, not only by TypeScript?
quiz.explain: JavaScript # private fields are truly private when the code runs.

quiz.q: What does implements Shape do?
options: Copies Shape methods into the class
Checks that the class matches the Shape interface
quiz.explain: implements is a compile-time check. It adds no code.

quiz.q: Can you write new Employee() if Employee is abstract?
quiz.explain: Abstract classes cannot be instantiated directly.

exercise.title: Payroll
exercise.prompt:
Write an abstract class `Employee` with a `name` field, an abstract method `pay(): number` and a method `describe(): string` returning `NAME (ROLE): PAY` where PAY is `pay()` with 2 decimals and ROLE comes from an abstract `role(): string`.

Subclasses:
- `Salaried` (role `salaried`): pay = yearly salary / 12
- `Hourly` (role `hourly`): pay = rate * hours

Input lines: `salaried NAME YEARLY` or `hourly NAME RATE HOURS`.

Print `describe()` for each employee, then `total: T` (2 decimals). Do not use constructor parameter properties.

lessons.title: Utility types
lessons.summary: Transform existing types with Partial, Required, Readonly, Pick, Omit, Record and ReturnType.

slides.title: Types from types
slides.text: TypeScript ships **utility types** that build new types from existing ones.
slides.narration:
You will often need a slightly different version of a type you already have.
Instead of copying it, use a utility type. Partial of Todo, for example, is the same shape but with every property optional, perfect for updates.

slides.title: Partial, Required, Readonly
slides.text:
- `Partial<T>`: all optional
- `Required<T>`: all required
- `Readonly<T>`: all readonly
slides.narration:
Partial, Required and Readonly change the modifiers of every property at once.
A function that applies changes to an object is the classic use of Partial.

slides.title: Pick and Omit
slides.text: Choose or drop properties by name.
slides.narration:
Pick keeps only the properties you name, and Omit keeps everything except the ones you name.
For example, a new todo has no id yet, because the database assigns it, so Omit of Todo and id describes it perfectly.

slides.title: Record, ReturnType, Awaited
slides.text:
- `Record` object with keys K - `ReturnType` what a function returns - `Awaited

` value inside a Promise
slides.narration:
Record with a union of keys forces you to provide a value for every key.
ReturnType extracts what a function returns, so you never have to repeat yourself.

slides.title: Under the hood: mapped types
slides.text: Utility types are written with **mapped types**.
slides.narration:
Utility types are not magic. They are mapped types, which loop over the keys of a type and build a new property for each one.
You can write your own, like Flags, which turns every property into a boolean.

quiz.q: What does Partial<T> do?
quiz.explain: Partial<T> adds ? to every property of T.

quiz.q: Which type removes the 'password' key from User?
quiz.explain: Omit<T, K> keeps all keys except K.

quiz.q: type S = Record<'a' | 'b', number>; Which value fits?
quiz.explain: Record requires exactly the listed keys, each with a number.

exercise.title: Applying partial updates
exercise.prompt:
Use this interface:
```typescript
interface Settings { theme: string; fontSize: number; autosave: boolean }
```
Start from the defaults `{ theme: 'light', fontSize: 14, autosave: true }`.

Input: one update per line as `key=value` (keys are `theme`, `fontSize`, `autosave`; autosave is `true`/`false`). Lines with an unknown key print `unknown key: KEY` and are skipped.

Build a `Partial<Settings>` from the valid lines, write `function applyUpdates(s: Readonly<Settings>, u: Partial<Settings>): Settings` that merges them (later lines win), and print the result as three lines `theme: ...`, `fontSize: ...`, `autosave: ...`.

tests.output:
unknown key: color
theme: light
fontSize: 18
autosave: false

unknown key: zoom
theme: light
fontSize: 14
autosave: true

lessons.title: keyof, typeof and indexed types
lessons.summary: Derive types from values and other types with typeof, keyof, indexed access and template literal types.

slides.title: typeof: types from values
slides.text: In a **type** position, `typeof value` gives the value's type.
slides.narration:
JavaScript's typeof gives a string at runtime. In a type position, TypeScript's typeof does something different: it gives you the full type of a value.
This lets you write the value once and derive the type from it.

slides.title: keyof: the property names
slides.text: `keyof T` is a union of T's keys.
slides.narration:
keyof takes an object type and gives you the union of its property names as literal types.
It is how you write functions that accept only valid property names.

slides.title: Indexed access
slides.text: `T['key']` reads the type of a property.
slides.narration:
Square brackets in a type read the type of a property, just like reading a value from an object.
Indexing with number reads the element type of an array or tuple, which is how we turn a list of constants into a union.

slides.title: Template literal types
slides.text: Build string types from other string types.
slides.narration:
Template literal types look like template strings, but they work on types.
Given unions, they produce every combination, which is great for describing naming patterns like CSS class names or event names.

slides.title: satisfies
slides.text: Check a value against a type **without** losing its precise type.
slides.narration:
Finally, the satisfies operator checks that a value matches a type, but keeps the more precise type that TypeScript inferred.
So you get validation and you still get autocomplete for the exact keys.

quiz.q: const c = { a: 1 }; In a type, what is typeof c?
quiz.explain: In a type position, typeof gives the full type of the value.

quiz.q: type T = { id: number; tags: string[] }; What is T['tags']?
quiz.explain: Indexed access reads the type of the tags property.

quiz.q: type E = `on-${'a' | 'b'}`; What is E?

lessons.title: Typing async code and errors
lessons.summary: Type promises and async functions, handle unknown errors safely, and model results with unions.

slides.title: Promise<T>
slides.text: An async function returning `T` has type `Promise<T>`.
slides.narration:
Asynchronous code works exactly as in JavaScript, and TypeScript adds types.
An async function that produces a number returns a Promise of number. When you await it, you get a plain number back.

slides.title: Typing a delay helper
slides.text: `new Promise<T>(...)` with a type argument.
slides.narration: When you build a promise yourself, give it a type argument. A promise that only signals completion is a Promise of void.

slides.title: Errors are unknown
slides.text: In `catch (err)`, `err` is **unknown**. Narrow it first.
slides.narration:
In JavaScript you can throw anything, not only Error objects. That is why the caught value is typed unknown in strict mode.
Check it with instanceof Error before reading its message.

slides.title: Results instead of exceptions
slides.text: Model success **or** failure as a discriminated union.
slides.narration:
Many TypeScript developers return a result object instead of throwing.
Because it is a discriminated union, the caller must check ok before using the value, so errors cannot be forgotten.

slides.title: Promise.all with tuples
slides.text: Types follow each position.
slides.narration: Promise all keeps the type of each position. Await an array of a string promise and a number promise, and you get a string and a number back.

quiz.q: What is the return type of async function f(): Promise<string>?
quiz.explain: Calling an async function always gives a Promise.

quiz.q: In strict mode, what is the type of err in catch (err)?
quiz.explain: Anything can be thrown, so the caught value is unknown and must be narrowed.

quiz.q: Why use a Result union instead of throwing?
options: The type forces callers to handle failure
Exceptions do not work in TS
quiz.explain: The caller must check ok before reaching value, so errors are not forgotten.

exercise.title: Async validation
exercise.prompt:

Write `async function validateAge(text: string): Promise<Result<number>>` that first awaits a short delay (`await wait(5)`), then returns:

- `{ ok: false, error: 'out of range' }` if the number is not an integer between 0 and 150
- otherwise `{ ok: true, value: n }`

Input: one value per line. Validate all lines **in parallel** with `Promise.all`, then print in input order `TEXT: valid` or `TEXT: ERROR`. Finally print `valid count: N`.

lessons.title: Modules, tsconfig and real projects
lessons.summary: Organize TypeScript into modules, use import type, configure tsconfig strict mode and type check your project.

slides.title: Modules with types
slides.text: Export types just like values. Use `import type` for type-only imports.
slides.narration:
TypeScript modules use the same import and export as JavaScript.
When you import something that is only a type, write import type. It tells tools the import can be erased completely, which type stripping requires.

slides.title: tsconfig.json
slides.text: The project's settings file. Start with **strict**.
slides.narration:
A tsconfig json file configures the compiler for a whole project.
Always turn on strict, which enables the most valuable checks. erasableSyntaxOnly and verbatim module syntax keep your code compatible with Node's type stripping.

slides.title: Type checking vs running
slides.text:
- `tsc --noEmit`: **check** types, produce nothing
- `node file.ts`: **run** (types stripped, not checked)
- Bundlers (Vite, esbuild) also strip types
slides.narration:
Remember that there are two separate jobs. Running TypeScript just strips the types. Checking types is done by tsc or by your editor.
In a real project you run tsc with no emit in your test or build step, so type errors never reach production.

slides.title: Types for libraries
slides.text: Many npm packages include types. Others have `@types/...` packages.
slides.code:
npm install --save-dev typescript @types/node
npx tsc --noEmit
slides.narration: Most popular packages ship their own type definitions. For others, the community maintains types in packages named at types slash something, such as at types slash node for Node's built-in modules.

slides.title: Good habits
slides.text:
- `strict: true`, avoid `any`
- Type the **edges** (inputs, outputs), let inference do the rest
- Validate outside data (`unknown` + narrowing)
- Derive types instead of duplicating them
slides.narration:
To finish the course, here are the habits that matter most. Keep strict mode on and avoid any.
Type your function boundaries and let inference handle the inside. Treat outside data as unknown until it is validated, and derive types from a single source of truth.

lessons.notes:
## Modules

TypeScript uses ES modules. Export values and types; import what you need:

```typescript
// geometry.ts
export type Point = { x: number; y: number };
export function distance(a: Point, b: Point): number {
  return Math.hypot(a.x - b.x, a.y - b.y);
}

// main.ts
import { distance } from './geometry.ts';
import type { Point } from './geometry.ts';
```

`import type` is erased completely. With `verbatimModuleSyntax`, TypeScript requires it for type-only imports, which keeps type stripping simple and predictable.

## tsconfig.json essentials

| Option | Why |
|---|---|
| `strict` | enables strict null checks, no implicit any and more |
| `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` | `arr[i]` may be `undefined` |
| `erasableSyntaxOnly` | forbids enums, namespaces, parameter properties |
| `verbatimModuleSyntax` | requires `import type` for types |
| `noEmit` | only type check (when Node or a bundler runs the code) |
| `allowImportingTsExtensions` | allows `'./file.ts'` imports |

## Workflow

```
npm init -y
npm install --save-dev typescript @types/node
npx tsc --init          # create tsconfig.json
npx tsc --noEmit        # type check
node src/main.ts        # run (Node 22.18+/23.6+ strip types by default)
```

## Declaration files

`.d.ts` files contain only types. Libraries publish them so your editor knows their API. `@types/*` packages provide them for libraries written in plain JavaScript.

## Migrating JavaScript

1. Rename files from `.js` to `.ts` one at a time.
2. Start with `strict: false` if needed, fix errors, then turn strict on.
3. Replace `any` with real types step by step.

## Where to go next

Frameworks like React, Angular, Vue, Express and NestJS all have first-class TypeScript support. You now have the foundations to read and write typed code in any of them.

quiz.q: What does import type do?
options: Imports only types and is fully erased
quiz.explain: Type-only imports disappear completely from the output.

quiz.q: Which command only checks types without producing files?
quiz.explain: --noEmit tells tsc to check and report errors only.

quiz.q: Where do types for a plain JavaScript library usually come from?
quiz.explain: The DefinitelyTyped project publishes @types/... packages.
